intro: Read the deck for the examples and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you something to remember and warns you where people slip. Rewrite a real paragraph of your own as you go, read your drafts aloud, and answer the recall questions without looking.

sections.title: Why Communication Matters in Development
sections.big_idea: In development, **clear writing is how evidence travels, money moves and people are heard**, and English is both a door and a gate.
in_plain_words: A programme nobody can describe clearly loses the grant, misses the policy window and confuses the community. The cost is real and rarely recorded, which is why writing gets little budget or training. Clarity buys trust, speed, influence and accountability, and the last matters most: a community cannot hold you to a document it cannot read.

English connects a field office to a funder and also shuts out staff, communities and local knowledge. **Use English as a tool and resist it as a hierarchy.** Writers in a second or third language start with an advantage, because the simple word is the plain word. This deck offers a toolkit of habits to use on Monday.

right.title: English closes
items: Speed and nuance in the field

key_terms.meaning: Simple, direct wording that the reader can follow first time.
A shared working language across many mother tongues.
Working in the language of the work and translating on purpose.
Specialist words used to signal status.
A community's ability to hold you to what you wrote.
A one-page version in the reader's own language.

worked_example.title: Count the cost of one vague email
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a vague email triggers three more emails to clarify it. A clear email gets one reply. A team sends 10 such vague emails.
steps: One vague email plus three clarifications: 1 + 3 = 4 emails.
Ten vague emails: 10 × 4 = 40 emails.
Ten clear emails: 10 × 1 = 10.
Emails saved by writing clearly: 40 − 10 = 30.
Add the community meeting nobody could follow, and the grant a reviewer put down after forty proposals.
worked_example.answer: Writing clearly saves 30 of 40 emails in the example, and the hidden costs are larger.

mistakes: Treating English as neutral infrastructure and ignoring who it excludes.
Treating English as pure imposition and ignoring what it opens.
Believing you need more vocabulary when you need fewer, plainer words.
Writing a report only in English when a one-page local summary would take an afternoon.

recall.q: Name two moments where unclear writing costs you.
recall.a: Any two of: a reviewer reading forty proposals, a brief arriving unreadable, three emails to clarify one, a meeting nobody could follow.

recall.q: Which benefit of clarity does the deck call the most important?
recall.a: Accountability: a community that can hold you to what you wrote.

recall.q: What does the deck say about writing in a second or third language?
recall.a: The habit of choosing the simple word is an advantage, because plain English is what the sector needs.

recall.q: What is the cheap counter to reports being only in English?
recall.a: A one-page summary in the local language.

recall.q: What does the deck say it is not?
recall.a: A grammar exam or a test of correct English; it is a working toolkit.

sections.title: The Plain-Language Revolution
sections.big_idea: Plain language passes a **three-part test**: the reader finds it, understands it first time, and can act on it.
in_plain_words: The plain-language movement holds that a document works if the intended reader can find what they need, understand it and use it, the first time. Only the middle part is about words. Most failures are in structure and in the missing ask. Complex writing often signals unfinished thinking, and the curse of knowledge makes experts skip steps.

Readable writing uses short sentences, common words, active voice, concrete nouns and clear layout. Aim for an average of 15 to 20 words a sentence. **Say who did what**, and use passive on purpose when the doer is unknown or the object is the point. Cutting the padding often halves the length.

diagram.caption: the plain-language test; most failures are first and third

key_terms.meaning: Writing the reader can understand the first time.
Forgetting what it is like not to understand.
A sentence that names who does what.
A sentence where the doer is hidden or absent.
A working target of 15 to 20 words.
A word like farmers or nurses that a reader can picture.

worked_example.title: Measure the plain rewrite
worked_example.setup: The deck's before sentence has 22 words and opens 'In order to...'. The after sentence, 'We changed how we deliver services so they help people more', has 11.
steps: Words cut: 22 − 11 = 11.
Share cut: 11 ÷ 22 = 50%.
Check the rhythm: the 15 to 20 target is an average over a page, so one short sentence is fine.
Check meaning: the after sentence says what changed and why.
Apply the same edit to one paragraph of your own report.
worked_example.answer: The rewrite cuts 11 words, half the sentence, and the meaning appears.

mistakes: Forgetting that only one of the three tests is about words; the point is often buried and the ask missing.
Writing every sentence at the same short length, so the page reads as a list.
Avoiding passive everywhere, when it suits an unknown doer or a methods section.
Taking readability scores as proof; they measure only sentence and word length.

recall.q: What are the three parts of the plain-language test?
recall.a: The reader finds what they need, understands it first time, and can act on it.

recall.q: What is the curse of knowledge?
recall.a: Once you understand something thoroughly, you forget what it is like not to, so you skip steps and definitions.

recall.q: What average sentence length does the deck recommend?
recall.a: 15 to 20 words, varied around the average.

recall.q: When is passive voice fine?
recall.a: When the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant, or the object is the point, or when protecting someone.

recall.q: What did the before and after example show?
recall.a: 22 words became 11, and the meaning appeared.

sections.title: Killing Development Jargon
sections.big_idea: Jargon is useful shorthand inside a team and **a fog outside it**: cut acronyms, abstractions, nominalisations and buzzwords.
in_plain_words: Every sector has a dialect. Used with a donor, journalist or community, it hides meaning. Four habits cause most of the fog: acronyms nobody spelled out, abstract nouns like beneficiaries and interventions, verbs turned into heavy nouns, and buzzwords like mainstream and capacity-build. Filler phrases pad every page.

The fix is a method: read aloud, circle, replace. **If you would not say it to a colleague over tea, do not write it in a report.** Replace abstractions with the people and actions they stand for, and spell out every acronym in every document. Some terms have a real technical sense, so test each before cutting.

children.label: Acronyms
items: Spell out on first use, every document
Never in titles or community materials

diagram.caption: each source with its plain fix

key_terms.meaning: Specialist words precise inside a group and opaque outside.
An abbreviation; spell it out on first use.
A general word that hides the real people and actions.
A strong verb turned into a heavy noun.
A fashionable word that conceals a choice.
Read aloud, circle, replace.

worked_example.title: Count words saved by plain phrases
worked_example.setup: Use five of the deck's phrase swaps. Count the words in each phrase and in its replacement, which is one word each.
steps: 'In order to' (3 words) becomes 'to': 3 − 1 = 2.
'Due to the fact that' (5) becomes 'because': 5 − 1 = 4.
'A large number of' (4) becomes 'many': 4 − 1 = 3.
'At this point in time' (5) becomes 'now': 5 − 1 = 4.
'In the event that' (4) becomes 'if': 4 − 1 = 3. Total saved: 2 + 4 + 3 = 9, and 4 + 3 = 7, so 9 + 7 = 16.
worked_example.answer: Sixteen words saved across the five phrases, with no loss of meaning.

mistakes: Using your own jargon with a donor, journalist or community as if it were shared.
Spelling out an acronym once in a series and assuming it afterwards.
Writing 'capacity was built' where 'we trained 30 nurses' can be counted.
Replacing a technical term without checking, such as mainstream in gender policy.

recall.q: What is the test for jargon in a case study?
recall.a: Would the woman in your case study recognise the words you use to describe her life?

recall.q: When should you spell out an acronym?
recall.a: On first use, in every document.

recall.q: What is nominalisation?
recall.a: Turning a strong verb into a heavy noun, such as implement into implementation.

recall.q: What are the three passes to cut jargon?
recall.a: Read aloud, circle -ation, -ment, buzzwords and acronyms, and replace with the word a colleague would use.

recall.q: Which pass does the deck call highest-yield?
recall.a: Reading aloud.

sections.title: Know Your Audience
sections.big_idea: Name your reader first: **the same finding gets different framing, vocabulary and length, and the number never changes**.
in_plain_words: Before writing, name the single reader, what they want from this, what they will do next and what would lose them. Donors want results and low risk, communities want respect, government wants policy alignment and protocol, media wants a story and a number. Formality and tone are separate dials, and clarity belongs to the pairing of word and reader.

Assume the reader is busy, on a phone, between meetings. Front-load the point and use headings that carry the message. **Rewrite for each audience without changing what is true.** Run the empathy test on any draft, and ask what does not serve the reader, because that question cuts length.

key_terms.meaning: How formal the language is, matched to reader and situation.
How the reader feels reading you, independent of formality.
The one person you write for first.
What the reader most wants from the document.
Four questions asked from the reader's side.
Putting the main point first.

worked_example.title: Reframe one finding for four readers
worked_example.setup: The deck's finding: enrolment rose 22% against a 15% target, within budget. Keep the number fixed and change only the framing.
steps: Donor: lead with target and budget. 22 − 15 = 7 points above target.
Community: say more of our children are in school than last year.
Government: say enrolment rose 22%, in line with the SSA targets for the block.
Media: say a village school raised girls' enrolment by more than a fifth in one year.
Check: could all four versions sit on one page without contradicting each other?
worked_example.answer: Four framings, one number: 22%, which is 7 points above the 15% target.

mistakes: Averaging the formality between readers instead of writing for the primary one.
Believing 'be less formal' fixes coldness, when formality and warmth are independent.
Using one word list for every reader; the same word fits one and walls out another.
Changing the number or the facts when you reframe for an audience.

recall.q: What four things should you name before writing?
recall.a: The single reader, what they want, what they will do next, and what would lose them.

recall.q: What do donors want?
recall.a: Results, value for money and low risk.

recall.q: What is the difference between formality and tone?
recall.a: Formality is how formal the language is; tone is how the reader feels reading you.

recall.q: What is the test for rewriting for a new audience?
recall.a: Could all versions sit on one page without contradicting each other?

recall.q: What do the four empathy questions end with?
recall.a: What does not serve them, which cuts length.

sections.title: Structure That Carries Meaning
sections.big_idea: Put the most important thing first: **bottom line, then key details, then background**, with every paragraph opening on its point.
in_plain_words: Even plain sentences fail in the wrong order. The inverted pyramid, borrowed from journalism, leads with the conclusion so the reader can stop at any point. BLUF puts the ask in the first sentence. Topic sentences open each paragraph, and three skim tests check the structure.

The executive summary is written last and must stand alone. Headings should say what is in the section. Link sentences by putting known information first and new information last. **Write in the order you thought, then reorder for the reader.** The two documents are different and both are needed.

levels.label: The bottom line
levels.sub: what you found, what you want

key_terms.meaning: Conclusion first, then key details, then background.
Bottom line up front: the ask or conclusion in sentence one.
The sentence that opens a paragraph with its main idea.
A one-page standalone summary, written last.
Headings and phrases that guide the eye.
Starting with the familiar and ending on the new idea.

worked_example.title: Re-order a buried request
worked_example.setup: Illustrative draft: three paragraphs of context, then at the end 'so we need ₹2 lakh by Friday.'
steps: Find the bottom line: the ask is ₹2 lakh by Friday.
Move it to the first sentence: 'We need ₹2 lakh by Friday to keep the clinic open.'
Follow with 'Here is why', then the key details.
Move the context into a short final background paragraph.
Run the skim test: first lines and headings alone should still carry the message.
worked_example.answer: Open with the ask and its deadline, then evidence, then background.

mistakes: Giving context for three paragraphs before the point.
Using 'Section 3' as a heading instead of 'What we found'.
Turning every paragraph into bullets, which strips the connectives.
Writing an executive summary that describes what the report does instead of what it found.

recall.q: What is the inverted pyramid?
recall.a: A structure that leads with the conclusion, then key details, then background.

recall.q: What are the three skim tests?
recall.a: First lines only, headings only, and summary only.

recall.q: When should the executive summary be written?
recall.a: Last, but it must stand alone.

recall.q: What does BLUF protect you from?
recall.a: A reader who stops after one line still receives the message.

recall.q: What is the known-to-new pattern?
recall.a: End a sentence with the new idea and start the next sentence with it.

sections.title: Everyday Professional Writing
sections.big_idea: Email is most of your writing: **one purpose, one ask, a named deadline, a subject line that works alone**.
in_plain_words: Your reputation grows one email at a time. A good subject line says what the message is and what you want. The body states the purpose in line one, makes one ask and gives a date instead of 'ASAP'. Requests are easier to grant when you give a reason and make it easy to say yes, and follow-ups restate the ask.

Minutes record decisions, actions, owners and deadlines, and what was deferred. Choose the channel by the record you need: WhatsApp for quick pings, email for decisions and money. **Short messages need one warm word**, especially upward and outward.

diagram.note: the deck's example: Field report submitted: review by Fri 12 June

key_terms.meaning: The only part guaranteed to be seen; says what and by when.
Urgency with no date, which the recipient decides for you.
A short close with name and role.
Decisions, actions, owners and deadlines.
WhatsApp for quick pings, email for records.
What you could need to find in two years.

worked_example.title: Rewrite a foggy email
worked_example.setup: The deck's before email: 'Hi, just wanted to touch base regarding the thing we discussed, it would be great if you could possibly look into it whenever you get a chance, no rush but kind of urgent.'
steps: Name the person: Ravi.
Replace 'the thing we discussed' with the document: the revised budget, attached.
Replace 'look into it' with a verb: approve.
Replace 'whenever you get a chance' with a date: Friday 12 June.
Give the reason: we cannot release funds without it.
worked_example.answer: 'Hi Ravi, could you approve the revised budget (attached) by Friday 12 June? We cannot release funds without it. Thanks!'

mistakes: Putting 'Update' or 'Important!!' in a subject line.
Sending four asks with none prominent.
Making a decision on WhatsApp and never recording it by email.
Writing 'Noted.' to a partner, which reads as displeasure.

recall.q: What should a strong subject line carry?
recall.a: What it is about, what is needed and by when.

recall.q: Why is 'ASAP' the least useful word in professional email?
recall.a: It communicates urgency without a date, so the recipient decides.

recall.q: What do good minutes record?
recall.a: Decisions, actions with owners, deadlines, and what was explicitly not decided.

recall.q: When should you use email instead of WhatsApp?
recall.a: For anything that needs a record, decisions, approvals, money, donors and government.

recall.q: How do you keep short messages from sounding cold?
recall.a: Add one warm word, such as 'Got it: thanks.'

sections.title: Grammar That Actually Trips People Up
sections.big_idea: Indian English is a valid variety: **fix the few recurring traps and treat the rest as audience choices**.
in_plain_words: The section starts with a reframe. Indian English is legitimate, and choosing international forms for a donor is a choice and no correction. Numbers need care, because an international donor will misread a crore. The traps that remain are narrow: subject and verb agreement, articles, a and an, tenses, prepositions and three punctuation marks.

Most have a mechanical test: find the real subject, check first mention against later mention, say the next word aloud, keep one tense per section. **Edit in passes, one issue each**, and ask a colleague. Grammar checkers are confident and sometimes wrong, so use them with care.

key_terms.meaning: A legitimate, fully grown variety with its own conventions.
The verb agrees with the real subject.
A, an or the; first mention takes 'a'.
Two sentences joined by a comma alone.
Hundred thousand and ten million; convert for donors.
One issue per pass.

worked_example.title: Convert and fix
worked_example.setup: A budget line reads 'Rs 5 crore'. A sentence reads 'One of the villages are in the pilot' and another 'We opened clinic in Patna'. The deck says a crore is ten million.
steps: Convert the amount: 5 × 10,000,000 = 50,000,000 rupees.
Give both forms for an international donor, as in the deck's 'Rs 5 crore (about USD 600,000)'.
Fix agreement: 'one of' is singular, so 'One of the villages is in the pilot'.
Fix the article: first mention takes 'a', so 'We opened a clinic in Patna'.
Edit in passes: agreement, then articles, then tense, then commas.
worked_example.answer: Rs 50,000,000, shown with its international figure; 'one of the villages is'; 'a clinic'.

mistakes: Calling 'prepone' or 'do the needful' an error when it is a choice by audience.
Letting a plural noun between subject and verb pull the verb into the plural.
Writing 'revert back' or 'discuss about'.
Trusting a grammar checker without reading, because it flags correct sentences.

recall.q: Why does the deck say Indian English is not broken English?
recall.a: It is a legitimate variety with its own valid conventions, like American or British English.

recall.q: How do you choose between a and an?
recall.a: By the sound of the next word: an NGO, a university.

recall.q: Which tense is used for what the data shows?
recall.a: Present simple.

recall.q: What should you do about lakh and crore for international donors?
recall.a: Always convert, because a misread crore is a factual error.

recall.q: What is the method for self-editing?
recall.a: Read aloud, one issue per pass, use a checker carefully, ask a colleague.

sections.title: Writing Reports & Briefs
sections.big_idea: A report is **the record** and a brief is **the persuasion**: write each for its job, and make every recommendation actionable.
in_plain_words: A project report has five parts: executive summary, context, what we did, findings and recommendations. Keep findings apart from interpretation so a reader can dispute your reading without disputing your data. A policy brief runs two to four pages and has a problem, evidence, options, ask and a reason to act now.

Strong paragraphs follow topic, evidence, takeaway, with the claim hedged to what the evidence supports. Cut until the point is clear, then stop. **A recommendation needs an actor, an action, a quantity and a date.** Run the checklist before you submit, and ask an outside reader to apply the last item.

right.title: Brief
items: The persuasion: one problem, key evidence

key_terms.meaning: The full record so the work can be checked and repeated.
Two to four pages built to move a decision.
Two sentences giving a reason to act this quarter.
Topic sentence, evidence, takeaway.
A causal suggestion that does not assert a cause.
Actor, action, quantity and date.

worked_example.title: Build the worked paragraph
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures: girls' enrolment rose from 180 to 220 against a 15% target.
steps: Topic: girls' enrolment rose sharply this year.
Growth in girls: 220 − 180 = 40.
Percentage rise: 40 ÷ 180 = 22.2%.
Target level: 180 × 0.15 = 27, so the target was 180 + 27 = 207; actual 220 − 207 = 13 above it.
Takeaway, hedged: the after-school transport scheme appears to be the main driver and is worth scaling.
worked_example.answer: A 22.2% rise, 13 girls above target, with a hedged takeaway.

mistakes: Writing an executive summary that says 'This report examines...'.
Shortening a report and calling it a brief.
Leaving the 'why now' out of a policy brief.
Writing recommendations such as 'strengthen the system' with no actor or date.

recall.q: What are the parts of a project report?
recall.a: Executive summary, context, what we did, findings and recommendations.

recall.q: How long is a policy brief?
recall.a: Two to four pages.

recall.q: What are the three beats of an analytical paragraph?
recall.a: Topic, evidence, takeaway.

recall.q: What does an actionable recommendation need?
recall.a: An actor, an action, a quantity and a date.

recall.q: What does a brief contain about method?
recall.a: A line at most.

sections.title: Communicating Data & Evidence in Words
sections.big_idea: Translate numbers into plain sentences, **keep precision honest**, and never let a verb claim a cause the data cannot show.
in_plain_words: Numbers do not speak for themselves. Round for prose, compare, anchor and give one number at a time. When you describe a chart, state the pattern, the key point and the exception. Keep the precise figure in tables and annexes.

A decimal is a claim about precision, so match the digits to the sample size. Qualifiers like 'about' and 'in this sample' are accuracy, while stacked hedges say nothing. Choose verbs that match your design: 'is linked with' where you might have written 'caused'. **Name the source, the date and the denominator.**

key_terms.meaning: Digits that claim accuracy the sample cannot support.
Expressing a share as 1 in 5 children.
A word like about or in this sample that scopes a claim.
The base a rate or share is calculated on.
A verb like raised or cut that asserts a cause.
Naming the source and date of a figure.

worked_example.title: Fix a false-precision sentence
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 'We found 47.3% of the 60 respondents used the service.' The deck says that is about 28 people.
steps: Convert the share to people: 60 × 0.473 = 28.4, so about 28.
The decimal point claims accuracy to a tenth of a percentage point.
Use whole numbers at this sample size: roughly half (28 of 60).
Name the scope: in this sample.
Name the source and year in brackets if it is a published figure.
worked_example.answer: 'Roughly half (28 of 60) respondents in this sample used the service.'

mistakes: Writing 'studies show' with no source or date.
Stacking hedges until the sentence says nothing.
Narrating every bar when describing a chart.
Turning 'incomes rose among those trained' into 'the training raised incomes'.

recall.q: What order should you follow to describe a chart?
recall.a: The overall pattern, the most important point, then the exception.

recall.q: What does a decimal point claim?
recall.a: A precision the sample size must support.

recall.q: Name two honest qualifiers.
recall.a: Any two of: about, roughly, in this sample, at least, appears to, is associated with, illustrative.

recall.q: What should you change in 'The training raised incomes' if you have no comparison group?
recall.a: Write 'Incomes rose among those trained'.

recall.q: What four things should a figure carry?
recall.a: The source name, the year, the denominator and whether it is your own estimate.

sections.title: Storytelling & Ethical Representation
sections.big_idea: Pair stories with numbers, and treat every story as **a person's life, told with consent, dignity and a say**.
in_plain_words: Numbers prove scale and stories create understanding. A good case study names a real person with consent, describes their situation, shows a concrete change and says what it shows. It illustrates a pattern and does not prove one. A composite is a fabrication unless labelled.

Avoid poverty porn: show strength and context. Use people-first language. Consent covers the story, name, photograph, venue and duration, and it must cost nothing to refuse. **Non-extractive practice lets people review their story first.** Before you publish, run the five-question check.

diagram.caption: the case study in four steps

key_terms.meaning: A story that illustrates a pattern but cannot prove it.
Exaggerated suffering used to provoke pity and donations.
Naming the person before the condition.
Permission for the story, name, photo, venue and duration.
Taking a story and returning nothing.
Sharing power so people shape how they appear.

worked_example.title: Check a story before publishing
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a draft says 'AIDS victims in a slum were helped.' It includes a named village, a photograph of a child, and no mention of consent.
steps: Language: 'AIDS victims' becomes 'people living with HIV'; 'slum' becomes 'informal settlement'.
Consent: ask separately for the story, the name and the photograph.
Child: take special care and get consent from those responsible.
Anonymity: a blurred face and a named village is not anonymity.
Show the person the draft first, and make declining costless.
worked_example.answer: Rewrite the language, get separate consent, protect the child and let the person review it.

mistakes: Presenting a composite case study as a real person.
Using consent to receive a service as consent to appear in a fundraising video.
Showing need alone, with no agency or choices.
Using identity-first or people-first language without checking a group's preference.

recall.q: What is poverty porn?
recall.a: Imagery or writing that exaggerates suffering to provoke pity and donations, stripping people of dignity.

recall.q: What must consent cover?
recall.a: Telling the story, name and photograph, where it appears, for how long, and the right to withdraw.

recall.q: What makes storytelling non-extractive?
recall.a: People review how they are shown, are quoted as said, and the community gets a copy and a say.

recall.q: What are the four steps of a case study?
recall.a: Person, situation, change and meaning.

recall.q: What is the sequencing of stories and numbers?
recall.a: The story makes the reader care and the number shows the case is not exceptional.

sections.title: Speaking, Presenting & Further Reading
sections.big_idea: The same rules hold on stage: **know the audience, lead with the point, keep it plain**, and slow down.
in_plain_words: A listener cannot go back, so announce the structure. Slides support the talk and do not replace it: one idea per slide, few words, the bottom line first, one ask at the end. An elevator pitch has four sentences, and Q&A rewards a pause and an honest 'I will follow up'.

In a second language, slow down, use short sentences, script the opening and closing, and skip the apology. Accent is fine. The reading list is short, led by Orwell's six rules and Plain English Campaign examples. **The best exercise is rewriting a page of your own.**

diagram.caption: five parts of the final section

key_terms.meaning: Who, what, proof and ask in about thirty seconds.
Announcing the shape, such as 'three things'.
One idea per slide, few words, large type.
Repeating the question briefly to confirm and buy time.
The essay's rules for clear writing.
Free guides and before-and-after examples.

worked_example.title: Time an elevator pitch
worked_example.setup: The deck says four sentences is about thirty seconds: who, what, proof, ask.
steps: Sentences in the pitch: 4.
Time per sentence: 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5 seconds.
Write the four sentences, one for each element.
Say them aloud a dozen times and time them.
Refresh the pitch once a year.
worked_example.answer: About 7.5 seconds a sentence; practise aloud until it holds.

mistakes: Reading your slides aloud.
Ending a talk with 'any questions?' and no ask.
Apologising for your English at the start.
Inventing a figure when you do not know.

recall.q: What do the deck's slide rules say about words?
recall.a: Few words in large type, one idea per slide, never read slides aloud.

recall.q: What does a pause before answering signal?
recall.a: Consideration, and it is not weakness.

recall.q: What are the four parts of an elevator pitch?
recall.a: Who, what, proof and ask.

recall.q: What does the deck say about accent?
recall.a: It is fine; speed and sentence length matter more.

recall.q: Which five takeaways does the deck close with?
recall.a: Clarity over cleverness, cut jargon, bottom line up front, your English is valid, a person behind every number.

notes.2: Eleven sections move from why communication matters, through plain language, jargon and audience, to structure, email, grammar, reports, data, stories and speaking. The roadmap on slide 10 shows how they group. Read section 2 first, because every later section applies its test.
notes.4: Unclear writing costs real things at real moments: a lost grant, a missed policy window, extra emails, community trust. The table pairs each cost with its moment. The last paragraph is the warning: **these losses are never recorded as communication failures**, which is why writing gets no budget.
notes.5: Read the two columns together: what goes wrong against what clarity buys. The fourth benefit is the one people forget, accountability, since a document a community cannot read is one they cannot use. **Treat clear writing as a governance practice** as well as a professional skill.
notes.6: English opens doors to funders, publication and networks, and closes them on non-English staff, community understanding and local knowledge. Both columns are true at once. The slide's practical answer is bilingual practice: **work in the language the work happens in** and translate on purpose.
notes.7: English can exclude, make jargon a status signal and favour the articulate over the right. The table pairs each exclusion with a cheap counter. The last row is cheap and rarely done: **a one-page summary in the local language takes an afternoon** and changes who can hold you to account.
notes.8: If you write in a second or third language, your habit of reaching for the simple word is an advantage, because plain English is what the sector needs. Your job is to get something done. The table reframes four worries. **Clarity beats fluency**: a short correct sentence beats a long broken one.
notes.9: The slide lists what the deck is: a practical toolkit, habits for Monday, confidence from method. Almost everything in it is a choice about word, order and reader. Anxiety about correctness is the main reason people write heavy, defensive prose, so **read the course as skills to use, with nothing to be graded on**.
notes.10: The roadmap has four stages: write plain, structure, get it right, communicate. Every example comes from real development writing, such as proposals, reports, emails and briefs. **Keep one real document of your own beside you** as you read, and apply each section to it.
notes.12: Plain language is a global standard with a three-part test: the reader finds what they need, understands it first time, and can act on it. Only the middle part is about words. Most failing documents fail on the **first and third**, because the point is buried and the ask is missing.
notes.13: Complex writing often signals unfinished thinking, a copied template or something being hidden. Clear writing is the last and hardest draft. Take Orwell's rule: cut any word you can. When a paragraph resists being made clear, **the problem is usually the idea** behind the words.
notes.14: The curse of knowledge hides from the person who has it. You forget what it is like not to know, so you skip definitions and steps. Write for the reader you were a year ago, and **give the draft to someone outside the programme** and ask what it is asking for.
notes.15: Five features make writing readable: short sentences, common words, active voice, concrete nouns and clear structure. Readability formulas measure only the first two, so a document can score well and still be unreadable. **Layout does more work than any sentence edit.**
notes.16: Read the chart for its direction only, since the figures are illustrative: longer words and sentences lower first-read comprehension. This matters for second-language readers and anyone in a hurry, **which is most of your audience**. Use the direction the research agrees on to set your habits.
notes.17: Aim for an average of 15 to 20 words a sentence and vary the rhythm around it. Sustained runs under 12 words feel choppy, and long ones over 35 need rereading. **Find the longest sentence on each page and split it.** Do that once per page and the average takes care of itself.
notes.18: Active voice names who did what. Passive often hides the actor, as in 'Mistakes were made.' The table shows where hiding hurts: decisions, errors, requests and follow-up. Test every sentence by asking who did this. If it cannot answer, **decide whether the omission is deliberate**.
notes.19: Passive has a place when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant, when the object is the point, or when you are protecting someone. The slide's advice is to **choose it on purpose and default to active**. Blanket passive-avoidance produces its own awkwardness.
notes.20: Compare the before and after: 22 words become 11, and the meaning finally appears. Each abstraction is replaced by the thing it stood for. **Try the same edit on one paragraph of your last report.** The slide says it takes ten minutes and teaches more than any advice.
notes.22: Jargon is shorthand inside your team and a fog outside it. The table ranks the effect by reader: useful for your team, noise for a donor, a different dialect for government, a wall for a community. Test it: **would the woman in your case study recognise your words** for her life?
notes.23: Spell out every acronym on first use in every document, because readers do not read in order. Add a list when you pass five, and keep acronyms out of titles, subject lines and community materials. **Read the example sentence aloud to someone outside your office** and watch their face.
notes.24: Abstract words hide the real thing: beneficiaries become farmers, interventions become the training or the clinic. Concrete wording can be checked, so 'we trained 30 nurses' can be counted and disputed. **Abstraction is where accountability leaks out.**
notes.25: Nominalisation turns a verb into a heavy noun and drops the actor, so 'we undertook the implementation of the plan' becomes 'we carried out the plan'. Scan for words ending in -ation, -ment, -ance and -ity. **Most can go back to verbs, and each conversion shortens the sentence.**
notes.26: Test each buzzword by swapping in the plain word. If nothing is lost, it did no work. The table shows what each hides: mainstream hides include routinely, capacity-build hides train, mentor or fund, low-hanging fruit hides easy wins. **Occasionally a term has a technical sense**, as 'mainstream' does in gender policy.
notes.27: Six phrases account for much of the padding: 'in order to' becomes 'to', 'due to the fact that' becomes 'because', 'a large number of' becomes 'many', and so on. This is find-and-replace work that needs no judgement. **Save the list as searches in your editor.**
notes.28: Watch how the jargon sentence loses meaning: every abstraction is swapped for something concrete, and a reader could repeat the result. 'At the grassroots level' adds no information and can almost always be deleted. The jargon version **means whatever the reader wants it to**.
notes.29: Three passes beat one careful edit, because each looks for one thing: read aloud, circle -ation, -ment, buzzwords and acronyms, then replace with the word a colleague would use. **Reading aloud is the highest-yield step in the course**, since almost every unclear sentence is audible before it is visible.
notes.31: Name your reader before writing: the one person, what they want in one line, what they will do next and what would lose them. Write the reader at the top of the draft and delete it before sending. With several readers, **write for the primary one** and add a short section for the others.
notes.32: Four readers, four hungers: donors want results and low risk, communities want respect and usefulness, government wants alignment and protocol, media wants a story and a number. The slide says practitioners handle government worst. **Ask a colleague with government experience to check your first letter.**
notes.33: The level of formality is a choice you make for a reader and a situation. The table gives three: formal, professional and informal. Getting it wrong is jarring in both directions. When unsure, **match the formality of the message you are replying to**, which costs no thought.
notes.34: Tone is how the reader feels reading you, and it is independent of formality. Aim to be confident, honest and human, and avoid boastful, apologetic and bureaucratic. With bad news, **say it plainly in the first line and then explain**. Burying it reads as evasion.
notes.35: One finding, four versions. Only the framing and vocabulary change; the number never does. Use the slide's check: could all four versions sit on one page without contradicting each other? If not, **one of them has drifted**. Each version leads with what that reader needs most.
notes.36: Assume a busy reader on a phone. Front-load the point, use headings that state content, keep paragraphs short and mark one ask. Test it: print the document and read only the headings and first lines. **If the message survives, the structure works.**
notes.37: A word that is clear to one reader is a wall to another. 'Disaggregated baseline' suits a donor and baffles a village meeting. Clarity belongs to the pairing of word and reader, which is why a universal blacklist fails. **Notice the gram sabha row**: local precision can be jargon abroad.
notes.38: Run four empathy questions on any draft: who opens this and why, what do they need in 30 seconds, which word would confuse them, what does not serve them. The fourth cuts length. **Audience-first writing takes longer to write and far less time to read.**
notes.40: Even plain sentences fail in the wrong order. The table lists the usual offenders: context first, the ask at the end, findings after method, recommendations in an annex. Order is invisible to the writer. **Write in the order you thought, then reorder for the reader.**
notes.41: The inverted pyramid leads with the conclusion, then key details, then background, so the reader can stop anywhere and still have the essentials. It comes from journalism, where a story could be cut from the bottom. **Use it for any report that will be read in a hurry.**
notes.42: BLUF puts the ask or conclusion in the first sentence. Compare the buried version with 'We need ₹2 lakh by Friday to keep the clinic open. Here is why...'. The objection that it feels abrupt concerns the writer's comfort. **A reader who stops after one line has still got the message.**
notes.43: Open each paragraph with its point, one idea per paragraph. Then run the three skim tests: first lines only, headings only, summary only. Each should still carry the message. They take five minutes on a finished draft and **catch structure problems that sentence editing cannot**.
notes.44: Write the executive summary last and make it stand alone: problem, what you did, what you found, what you recommend. It must fit one page and add no new information. **A summary that describes what the report does is a table of contents in prose.** Lead with findings.
notes.45: Use headings that state content ('What we found'), signpost phrases, bullets only for parallel items and white space. A reader should be able to move through your document by headings alone. Turning prose into bullets removes the connectives that carried the argument, so **use bullets sparingly**.
notes.46: Link sentences by putting known information first and new information last, then starting the next sentence with that new idea. Transitions such as 'but', 'so' and 'because' tell the reader how ideas relate. **A 'however' between two unconnected sentences connects nothing.**
notes.48: Emails are most of your writing, and your reputation grows one message at a time. The table lists what a good email has: one purpose, one ask, a named deadline and a subject line that works alone. A vague email is paid for twice, in **the follow-up thread**.
notes.49: Write the subject line to say what it is, what you want and by when. Compare the weak column with the strong one. A subject line is read in a list of forty on a phone, and it is how the message is found again. **'Update' is unsearchable.**
notes.50: A clean email has a greeting that matches the relationship, the purpose in line one, one ask, a real deadline and a sign-off with your name and role. Replace 'ASAP' with a date. With four asks, **number them and say so in the first line**, then re-read once.
notes.51: When you ask, say what you need and by when, make it easy to say yes by attaching or pre-filling, and give a reason. When you chase, wait a reasonable time, assume goodwill and **restate the ask and the deadline** so the reader need not scroll back.
notes.52: Good minutes record decisions, actions with owners and deadlines, and what was explicitly not decided. Leave out who said what and the discussion. The last row stops the same conversation recurring. **Circulate within a day**: minutes sent that evening are a management tool.
notes.53: Use WhatsApp for quick yes or no, field coordination and time-critical pings, and email for records, decisions, money, donors and government. The test: would you want to find it in two years? **Where a decision happened on WhatsApp, email it afterwards in one line.**
notes.54: See what changed in the foggy email: a named person, the document, a verb they can act on, a date, and one clear urgency. The rewrite is just as warm. 'No rush but kind of urgent' tells the reader nothing, and **a date tells them everything**.
notes.55: Short messages can read as curt, so add one warm word. Compare 'Got it: thanks' with 'Noted.' The risk is greatest upward and outward, where a brusque message reads as displeasure. **Clarity and warmth go together**, so be brief and kind.
notes.57: Indian English is a legitimate variety with its own valid conventions. For an international donor you may choose international forms, which is a matter of audience fit and carries no correction. Convert numbers too: **give an international figure beside any lakh or crore**.
notes.58: Find the real subject and ignore what sits between it and the verb. 'Each' and 'one of' are singular however many nouns follow. 'Data' as a singular is widely accepted, though some journals still want the plural. **Match the house style of where you are sending it.**
notes.59: Use a or an for something new and one of many, the for something specific the reader can identify, and no article for general plurals and uncountables. A quick check: first mention takes 'a', later mentions take 'the'. That rule alone **resolves the majority of cases** in ordinary prose.
notes.60: Choose a or an by the sound of the next word, whatever its spelling. Say it aloud: 'an NGO' because N is pronounced 'en', 'a university' because it starts with a 'y' sound. **This is one of the few mechanical rules in English**, so let your ear decide.
notes.61: Match tense to job: past simple for what you did, present simple for what the data shows, present continuous for ongoing work, future for what you will do. Do one editing pass for tense alone. **Watch the causal wording** in 'Female literacy lowers fertility': slide 81 would write 'is linked with'.
notes.62: Prepositions are learned phrase by phrase, so there is no rule to derive. The table lists common slips: discuss the plan, comprise three parts, cope with the load, different from last year. **Keep a personal list of the five you get wrong most** and check for them specifically.
notes.63: Indian and international English are both valid, and the right-hand column avoids confusion for an international funder. Context decides. The last row is the only one that is not a style choice: **always convert lakh and crore for donors**, because a misread crore is a factual error in a budget.
notes.64: Three marks to get right: avoid the comma splice, use its for belonging and it's for it is, and use semicolons sparingly to join two full sentences. Each has a one-second test. **When in doubt use a full stop**, since two short sentences are never wrong.
notes.65: Edit in passes: read aloud, then one issue per pass (articles, tenses, commas), then use a checker with care, then ask a colleague. Trying to catch everything in one read loses attention after the first error. **Checkers flag correct sentences and miss whole categories of error.**
notes.67: A project report has five parts, and the table gives the question each answers. Lead with findings and recommendations, with method and context in support. **Keep findings apart from interpretation**, so a reader can accept your data and dispute your reading. Cut context the findings do not need.
notes.68: A policy brief runs two to four pages for a decision-maker with minutes to spare: a one-paragraph problem, half a page of evidence with a chart, specific numbered recommendations and two sentences on why now. **Write the recommendation first** and build the brief to support it.
notes.69: A brief is a different document from a report, with a different job. The report is the record so the work can be checked, and the brief is the persuasion so action can be taken. Producing one by cutting the other yields neither. **Write both when the work warrants it.**
notes.70: A strong analytical paragraph has three beats: topic sentence, evidence, takeaway. Weak paragraphs usually miss the third and leave the reader to find the significance. The takeaway is also where over-claiming enters, so **say what the evidence supports and no more**.
notes.71: The worked paragraph is three sentences: the claim, the numbers (180 to 220 against a 15% target) and a hedged takeaway. 'Appears to be the main driver' suggests a cause without asserting one. **Weak paragraphs in this genre are often these same three ideas spread over eight sentences.**
notes.72: Cut until the point is clear, then stop. Delete the first sentence if it is a warm-up, keep one idea per paragraph and ask each sentence what it is for. The chart is illustrative. **There is a floor**: cutting past the reader's minimum context pushes the work back onto them.
notes.73: A recommendation needs an actor, an action, a quantity and a date. Compare each vague line with its actionable version. Miss any element and it cannot be accepted, refused or tracked. **Naming the actor feels presumptuous and makes the recommendation real.**
notes.74: Run this checklist before you submit: summary stands alone, acronyms spelled out, one point per paragraph, recommendations owned and timed, nothing kept for sounding clever. It takes ten minutes and catches much of what a reviewer would send back. **The last item needs an outside reader.**
notes.76: Numbers do not speak for themselves, so translate them into plain sentences without distorting them. 'MPCE of Rs 2,700 (median)' becomes 'half of households spend less than Rs 2,700 a head'. Where plainness would lose precision, **keep the number and add the plain version beside it**.
notes.77: To describe a chart, state the overall pattern, then the most important point, then the exception. Do not narrate every bar, read axis labels aloud or describe colours. **If you cannot state the pattern in one sentence**, the chart is probably showing too much and should be split.
notes.78: Four techniques make numbers readable: round for prose, compare, anchor, and use one number at a time. 'One in five children' is imaginable, while twenty per cent is arithmetic. **Keep the precise figure in tables** and the annex, where it matters.
notes.79: A decimal is a claim about precision. Writing 47.3% from 60 respondents pretends to accuracy the data cannot support, and 'roughly half (28 of 60)' is honest. Use the sample-size table: **whole numbers at 60, whole points at 600**, and a decimal at 6,000 only sometimes.
notes.80: Qualifiers are accuracy, as long as they are specific. 'About', 'in this sample', 'at least', 'appears to' and 'illustrative' each tell the reader how far to trust a number. **Do not stack hedges**: 'may possibly indicate a potential trend' says nothing.
notes.81: The verb is where overclaiming hides: 'raised', 'reduced' and 'cut' assert a cause. Unless you ran a proper evaluation with a comparison group, write 'is linked with' or 'followed'. **Say what you observed and, separately, what you think explains it.**
notes.82: Name the source, give the date, state the denominator and flag your own estimates. 'Studies show' is the weakest phrase in evidence writing. A number that turns out to be invented does more damage than a gap. **Cite the way the slide does: '(NFHS-5, 2019–21)'.**
notes.84: Numbers prove scale and stories create understanding, so pair them. The sequence matters: the story makes the reader care and the number shows the case is typical. A story without a number is an anecdote, and **a number without a story is rarely acted on**.
notes.85: A good case study follows four steps: a real named person, their situation, a concrete change and what it shows. It illustrates a pattern and proves nothing alone. A composite is a fabrication unless you **say so in the main text**, where readers will see it.
notes.86: Poverty porn exaggerates suffering to win pity and donations. The test is whether the reader is left with pity or respect. The table swaps each mechanism for an alternative: a name, context, action and agency. **Show strength, choices and context** alongside need.
notes.87: Consent in storytelling is separate from consent to receive a service. It must cover the story, the name and photograph, where it will appear, for how long and the right to withdraw. **Consent that costs the person something to refuse is not consent.** Take extra care with children and survivors.
notes.88: Put the person before the condition: 'people living in poverty', 'women who have not had schooling'. Language that defines people by their hardship removes dignity. The slide adds a caution: some communities prefer identity-first language, so **follow a group's stated preference**.
notes.89: Extractive storytelling takes a community's pain, packages it and returns nothing. Non-extractive practice shares power: people review how they appear, their words are quoted as said, and the community gets a copy and a say. **Showing people their story before publication also improves accuracy.**
notes.90: Use this as a gate before you publish: consent, dignity and agency, recognition, with versus from, and what the community gets back. If any answer is no or unsure, **stop and fix it first**. The five questions are the whole section in checklist form.
notes.92: Speaking follows the same principles: know your audience, lead with the point, keep it plain. A listener cannot go back, so announce the structure, such as 'I will cover three things'. The table translates written tools into spoken ones. **Say the ask in the first ten seconds.**
notes.93: Slides support the talk. Use one idea per slide, few words in large type, open with the bottom line and end with one ask. If your slides could be emailed and fully understood, you are not needed. **Prepare for the deck failing**, so the talk survives a dead projector.
notes.94: An elevator pitch has four sentences: who, what, proof and ask. That is about thirty seconds. Write it down, say it aloud a dozen times and refresh it yearly. **The ask is the part people omit**, and its absence is why conversations end politely with nothing following.
notes.95: Under pressure: pause, restate the question, answer the one asked, keep it short. If you do not know, say so and offer to follow up. 'I do not know, I will send it by Friday' is remembered as reliability. **Never invent a figure.**
notes.96: Presenting in a second language: slow down, use short sentences, script the opening and closing and improvise the middle. Do not apologise for your English, because it cues the audience to listen for errors. **Speed and sentence length drive clarity**, and both improve with one rehearsal.
notes.97: Five items on the shelf: Strunk and White for brevity, Orwell for the six rules, the Plain English Campaign for free examples, Zinsser for warmth and Williams for clarity. The slide's last row is serious: **rewrite one page of your own writing** with this course open beside you.
notes.98: Orwell's six rules come with a modern equivalent for each. The sixth keeps them usable: break any rule sooner than write something barbarous. The deck calls the essay the best one-page writing course. **Print the list** and run it as the final pass on a draft.
notes.99: Five takeaways: clarity over cleverness, cut jargon, bottom line up front, your English is valid, and a person behind every number. All five are habits, so they improve with repetition. **If you adopt one, read your drafts aloud**: it catches unclear sentences, missing words and jargon in one pass.
